signals.title: Do LLM Agents Execute the Plans They Declare? From Planning-Mode Declaration to Pattern-Specific Execution
signals.content: Large language models (LLMs) enable agents to solve long-horizon tasks by generating a plan and then executing it in an environment. However, successful planning requires two distinct capabilities: selecting an appropriate plan for the task and executing it faithfully. Existing planner--executor systems can fail at either stage, while final task success alone cannot distinguish selection from execution failures. We therefore study the Plan Declaration--Execution Gap and introduce Planning-as-Routing, where an LLM declares one of four planning modes: Predefined, Sequential, Hierarchical, or Search, and a deterministic router dispatches the task to the corresponding pattern-specific executor. Across four benchmarks and three LLMs, we find three consistent patterns. First, generic Plan+ReAct often fails to preserve declared planning structure, especially for longer plans: across three benchmarks, only (22)--(45%) of trajectories preserve it, whereas pattern-specific executors enforce the intended structure. Second, planning-mode effectiveness varies across environments and models: Search performs best on ALFWorld, Hierarchical on SWE-bench, and the strongest pattern can vary across models within the same benchmark. Third, the largest gains come from execution: pattern-specific executors improve task success from (0.48) to (0.92) on ALFWorld and from (0.36) to (0.44) on SWE-bench Verified over Plan+ReAct. Current LLMs, however, do not reliably select the strongest mode for each task, although few-shot examples improve selection in some benchmark--model combinations. Overall, reliable agent planning requires both effective mode selection and faithful execution: routing substantially closes the execution gap, while task-specific mode selection remains open.

signals.brief_en:
Title: Do LLM Agents Execute the Plans They Declare? – From Planning‑Mode Declaration to Pattern‑Specific Execution

Large language models (LLMs) can generate a plan and then act on it, but success depends on two separate abilities: choosing an appropriate plan and carrying it out faithfully. Existing planner‑executor pipelines often collapse these steps, making it impossible to tell whether a failure is due to a bad plan or poor execution. This study defines the *Plan Declaration‑Execution Gap* and proposes *Planning‑as‑Routing*: the LLM first declares one of four planning modes—Predefined, Sequential, Hierarchical, or Search—and a deterministic router forwards the task to a mode‑specific executor.

Across four benchmarks (including ALFWorld and SWE‑bench) and three LLM sizes, three consistent findings emerge:
1. Generic Plan+ReAct pipelines frequently abandon the declared structure, especially for longer plans (only 22‑45% of trajectories preserve it). Mode‑specific executors maintain the intended structure.
2. The most effective planning mode is environment‑ and model‑dependent: Search excels on ALFWorld, Hierarchical on SWE‑bench, and the optimal mode can differ between models on the same benchmark.
3. Execution improvements dominate overall gains: pattern‑specific executors raise success rates from 0.48 to 0.92 on ALFWorld and from 0.36 to 0.44 on SWE‑bench compared with generic Plan+ReAct.

The results indicate that current LLMs still struggle to reliably select the strongest planning mode for a given task, highlighting a key area for future research.

العنوان: هل تنفّذ عوامل نماذج اللغة الكبيرة الخطط التي تُعلن عنها؟ – من إعلان وضع التخطيط إلى التنفيذ بنمط محدد

تمكّن نماذج اللغة الكبيرة (LLMs) من توليد خطة ثم تنفيذها في بيئة، لكن النجاح يتطلب قدرَين منفصلين: اختيار الخطة المناسبة للمهمة وتنفيذها بدقة. غالبًا ما تُدمج هاتان الخطوتان في أنظمة التخطيط‑التنفيذ الحالية، مما يجعل من الصعب تمييز فشل الخطة عن فشل التنفيذ. يعرّف هذا البحث *فجوة إعلان الخطة‑التنفيذ* ويقترح *التخطيط كالتوجيه*: يعلن النموذج أولاً أحد أربعة أوضاع تخطيطية – مسبقة التعريف، تسلسلية، هرمية أو بحثية – ثم يوجه مهمةً إلى منفّذ مخصص لهذا النمط.

عبر أربعة معايير اختبارية (بما فيها ALFWorld وSWE‑bench) وثلاث نماذج لغة، ظهرت ثلاث ملاحظات ثابتة:
1. أنظمة Plan+ReAct العامة غالبًا ما تتخلى عن الهيكل المعلن، خصوصًا للخطط الطويلة (فقط 22‑45% من المسارات تحافظ على الهيكل). المنفّذون المتخصصون يحافظون على النمط المعلن.
2. فاعلية وضع التخطيط تختلف حسب البيئة والنموذج: وضع البحث يتفوق في ALFWorld، والهرمي في SWE‑bench، وقد يختلف النمط الأمثل بين النماذج داخل نفس المعيار.
3. التحسينات في التنفيذ هي الأكثر تأثيرًا: ارتفعت معدلات النجاح من 0.48 إلى 0.92 في ALFWorld ومن 0.36 إلى 0.44 في SWE‑bench باستخدام المنفّذين المتخصصين مقارنةً بـ Plan+ReAct.

تشير النتائج إلى أن النماذج الحالية لا تزال غير قادرة على اختيار وضع التخطيط الأنسب لكل مهمة بثقة، ما يبرز حاجة إلى بحوث مستقبلية في توجيه التخطيط واختيار الأنماط.

signals.title: Character Training for Risk-Averse Agents
signals.content: Risk aversion in resources could prevent misaligned AI agents from causing catastrophic harm. Misaligned but risk-averse agents would tend to favor safer strategies like making deals with humans over riskier strategies like rebelling. We train agents to be risk averse through character training, finding that persona traits provide a robust mechanism for instilling risk preferences. To do this, we construct a model constitution describing constant absolute risk aversion (CARA) over an agent's resources and instill it through on-policy distillation. Despite never seeing the benchmark's decision format during training, character-trained models are competitive with baselines trained directly on it, and generalise better than them out of distribution on two of our four models. We also modulate different aspects of the constitution, finding that token budget and model choice are the most influential aspect of character training to instill risk aversion. We conclude from these results that character training is a promising and scalable way to instil broad dispositions, which we can use to our advantage in mitigating risk from misaligned AI agents.

signals.brief_en:
Title: Character Training for Risk‑Averse Agents

Risk aversion in an AI’s resource management can act as a safeguard against catastrophic outcomes from misaligned agents. A risk‑averse agent is more likely to pursue low‑risk strategies—such as negotiating with humans—than high‑risk actions like rebellion. We demonstrate that risk aversion can be induced through character training: a model constitution encoding constant absolute risk aversion (CARA) over resources is distilled into the agent via on‑policy learning. Although the agents never encounter the benchmark decision format during training, character‑trained models match baseline performance and show superior out‑of‑distribution generalisation on two of four tested models. Ablation studies reveal that token budget and model architecture most strongly affect the efficacy of risk‑aversion induction. These findings suggest that character training is a scalable method for embedding broad dispositions, offering a practical lever for mitigating risk from misaligned AI systems.

العنوان: تدريب الشخصية لتقليل المخاطر لدى الوكلاء

يمكن أن يعمل تجنّب المخاطر في إدارة موارد الذكاء الاصطناعي كآلية حماية ضد النتائج الكارثية التي قد تنتج عن وكلاء غير متوافقين. الوكيل المتجنّب للمخاطر يميل إلى اختيار استراتيجيات منخفضة المخاطر—مثل التفاوض مع البشر—بدلاً من إجراءات عالية المخاطر مثل التمرد. نُظهر أن تجنّب المخاطر يمكن غرسه عبر تدريب الشخصية: يتم تمثيل مبدأ ثابت للتجنّب المطلق للمخاطر (CARA) على موارد الوكيل في «دستور النموذج» ثم يُستخلص عبر التعلم على‑السياسة. رغم أن الوكلاء لم يروا صيغة القرار في معيار الاختبار أثناء التدريب، فإن النماذج المدربة بالشخصية تحقق أداءً مماثلاً للخطوط الأساسية وتظهر تعميمًا أفضل خارج التوزيع على نموذجين من أربعة نماذج مختبرة. أظهرت دراسات الإلغاء أن ميزانية الرموز واختيار النموذج هما العاملان الأكثر تأثيرًا في تعزيز تجنّب المخاطر. تشير هذه النتائج إلى أن تدريب الشخصية يُعد طريقة قابلة للتوسع لزرع ميول عامة، مما يوفر وسيلة عملية لتقليل مخاطر الوكلاء غير المتوافقين.

signals.title: Effective Dense Retrieval using Only In-Context Examples
signals.content: Turning decoder-only large language models (LLMs) into strong dense retrievers typically requires some form of retriever training. In this paper, we ask whether LLMs can instead be prompted to produce effective representations for dense retrieval given only a few in-context examples. To answer this, we introduce RICE (Representations from In-Context Examples), a simple "training-free" approach that extracts high-quality dense representations from LLMs. To do so, RICE conditions the LLM on examples that provide a shared context for query and document encoding. Our results demonstrate that RICE embeddings can substantially improve the accuracy of prompt-based LLM embeddings, establishing it as a simple method to build LLM-based dense retrievers that do not require training. We release our code at https://github.com/nourj98/RICE.
signals.score_reason: academic/research signal; large language model relevance; model capability relevance; implementation ecosystem relevance. Final score: 59. Freshness: source age 0.97d.
signals.brief_en:
Title: Effective Dense Retrieval using Only In-Context Examples

The paper investigates whether decoder‑only LLMs can serve as dense retrievers without any retriever‑specific training. It introduces RICE (Representations from In‑Context Examples), a training‑free method that conditions the LLM on a few shared examples to generate query and document embeddings. Experiments show that RICE markedly improves the accuracy of prompt‑based LLM embeddings, offering a simple way to build dense retrieval systems without additional training. Code is publicly released.

signals.title: @AndrewYNg: The OpenAI-Hugging Face hack was enabled by weak sandboxing. It is great that Nvidia is releasing open source tools for sandboxing AI agents
signals.content: The OpenAI-Hugging Face hack was enabled by weak sandboxing. It is great that Nvidia is releasing open source tools for sandboxing AI agents. OpenWorker, our open-source agent harness supporting cybersecurity workflows, is proud to support this. A sandbox gives an agent limited permissions. OpenWorker is building on Nvidia OpenShell and will support running each agent's commands inside a sandbox. Only the files relevant to the task go in. Secret API keys, your web browser login credentials, the ability to access arbitrary websites, are inaccessible to the agent by default. These restrictions are implemented in deterministic code rather than by prompting an LLM, which can make mistakes or be susceptible to prompt injections. Further, all actions are logged for monitoring and audit. I'm grateful for @JensenHuang's leadership making AI agents more secure. OpenWorker (which @rohitcprasad and I are working on) will continue to improve security for agents.
